learning_design.unlock_rule: A knowledge node unlocks after all required prompts are completed, including required code or table discoveries.
learning_design.mastery_note: Discovery progress is not mastery evidence; progressively harder retrieval and typed coding questions provide the scored signal.

authoring_notes: Domain 1 quality pass: expanded each knowledge node into short, ADHD-friendly progressive explanations plus an annotated code example. Each code page now has one high-value click-to-reveal runtime result (console output or resulting value) so learners connect syntax with behavior. Progressive text hides one key phrase normally and no more than two. Glossary terms are scoped per node and only explain supporting vocabulary, not the page topic. Facts were revalidated against Python 3.14 documentation while preserving compatibility with the track's Python 3.10-3.14 scope.

reveal.text: `zip()` returns a lazy iterator that pulls from each input iterable in parallel.

prompts.label: READ PARALLEL ITERATION
prompts.placeholder: Click the important parts. zip pairs items by position.

reveal.code:
names = ["Ada", "Linus", "Grace"]
scores = [98, 91, 95]

for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

annotations.title: Pair iterables by position
annotations.explanation: zip yields one tuple from the same position of each iterable.

annotations.title: Unpack each pair
annotations.explanation: The tuple from zip is unpacked directly into name and score.

reveal.text: Plain `zip()` stops at the shortest iterable; `strict=True` raises `ValueError` when lengths differ.

prompts.label: WHEN SHOULD STRICT MODE BE USED?

reveal.text: Use `strict=True` when unequal lengths indicate a bug; omit it when intentional truncation is acceptable.

glossary.definition: Work is delayed until values are requested instead of producing every result immediately.

reveal.text: `*pairs` expands each pair as a positional argument to `zip()`, which can transpose rows into columns.

prompts.label: READ THE TRANSPOSE IDIOM
prompts.placeholder: Click *pairs and zip. Rows become arguments, then zip regroups by position.

annotations.title: Expand rows into arguments
annotations.explanation: * passes each pair as a separate positional argument to zip.

annotations.title: Transpose the pairs
annotations.explanation: zip groups all first elements together and all second elements together.

reveal.text: `zip(*pairs)` returns an iterator whose grouped outputs are tuples when consumed.
If `pairs` is empty, `names, scores = zip(*pairs)` fails because there are no columns to unpack.

glossary.definition: A function-call argument matched to a parameter by its position.
Swap rows and columns so values that shared a position are grouped together.
An object that produces one item at a time when Python asks for the next value.
An ordered, immutable collection of values, usually written with commas.

annotations.title: Choose the first index

Use `enumerate()` instead of maintaining a manual counter beside a loop.

prompts.label: HOW DO MULTIPLE FOR CLAUSES WORK?

reveal.text: Multiple `for` clauses in a comprehension follow the same order as equivalent nested loops.

prompts.label: TRACE THE LOOP ORDER
prompts.placeholder: Read the clauses left to right as nested loops.

reveal.code:
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]

flat = [
    value
    for row in matrix
    for value in row
]

annotations.title: Outer loop
annotations.explanation: The first for-clause iterates rows.

annotations.title: Inner loop
annotations.explanation: For each row, the second clause iterates values.

reveal.text: Read the outer loop first, then the inner loop, then each filter at the level where it appears.
If a nested comprehension becomes hard to scan, explicit loops are often clearer.

glossary.definition: The loop that runs first and contains another loop.
The loop that runs inside an outer loop.
A condition that decides which candidate values are kept.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES A DICT COMPREHENSION BUILD?

reveal.text: A dictionary comprehension creates a key-value pair for each item that reaches its output expression.

prompts.label: BUILD KEY-VALUE PAIRS
prompts.placeholder: Click the key:value expression and filter.

annotations.title: Key/value expression
annotations.explanation: This expression defines one dictionary entry for each kept item.

annotations.title: Optional filter
annotations.explanation: Only words satisfying the condition produce entries.

reveal.text: If the comprehension produces the same key more than once, the later value replaces the earlier value.

prompts.label: KEYS MUST WORK AS DICTIONARY KEYS

reveal.text: Dictionary keys must be hashable; a list cannot be used directly as a dictionary key.

glossary.definition: One dictionary entry: a key used for lookup and its associated value.
Able to produce a stable hash value, which is required for dictionary keys and set members.
A condition that decides which candidate values are kept.

reveal.text: `next(iterator, default)` returns the next item, or the default when the iterator is exhausted.

prompts.label: FIND THE FIRST MATCH SAFELY
prompts.placeholder: Click the lazy generator and default.

reveal.code:
users = [
    {"name": "Ada", "active": False},
    {"name": "Grace", "active": True},
]

first_active = next(
    (user for user in users if user["active"]),
    None,
)

anchor.text: user for user in users if user["active"]

annotations.title: Lazy matching
annotations.explanation: The generator yields matching users one at a time.

annotations.title: Default value
annotations.explanation: If no match is yielded, next returns None instead of raising StopIteration.

reveal.text: Combine `next()` with a generator expression to stop at the first matching item without building a list.
Calling `next()` on an exhausted iterator without a default raises `StopIteration`.

glossary.definition: An object that produces one item at a time when Python asks for the next value.
A compact expression such as `(x for x in items)` that produces values lazily.
The exception an exhausted iterator raises when `next()` is called without a default.
Work is delayed until values are requested instead of producing every result immediately.

reveal.text: An assignment expression stores a value inside an expression and also returns that same value.

prompts.label: ASSIGN WHILE TESTING
prompts.placeholder: Click := and then see how the value is reused.

annotations.title: Assignment expression
annotations.explanation: := both stores the expression result and yields it to the condition.

annotations.title: Reuse the bound value
annotations.explanation: The body can use message without recomputing the expression.

reveal.text: Use `:=` when one computed value must be tested and reused without recomputing it.
Inside a comprehension `if` clause, wrap an assignment expression in parentheses.

glossary.definition: Python code that evaluates to a value.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES * DO IN A CALL?

reveal.text: In a function call, `*values` expands an iterable into positional arguments.

reveal.code:
def distance(x, y):
    return (x**2 + y**2) ** 0.5

point = (3, 4)
result = distance(*point)

annotations.title: Positional unpacking
annotations.explanation: * expands the tuple so distance receives 3 as x and 4 as y.

prompts.label: THE CALL STILL HAS TO FIT

reveal.text: The expanded item order and count must still match what the callable accepts positionally.
The variable does not need to be named `args`; `*point` and `*dimensions` use the same unpacking syntax.

glossary.definition: An object you can loop over, such as a list, tuple, string, range, or generator.
A function-call argument matched to a parameter by its position.
An object that can be called with parentheses, such as a function, method, or class.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES ** DO IN A CALL?

reveal.text: In a function call, `**mapping` expands mapping entries into keyword arguments.

annotations.title: Keyword unpacking
annotations.explanation: Mapping keys become keyword names and mapping values become argument values.

reveal.text: Keys supplied through `**mapping` in a function call must be strings.
If the same parameter receives a value twice, the function call raises `TypeError`.

glossary.definition: An object that associates keys with values. A dictionary is the most common mapping.
A function-call argument matched to a parameter by name.
An exception commonly raised when an operation receives an object or argument combination of an inappropriate type or form.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES ** DO INSIDE A DICTIONARY?

reveal.text: Inside a dictionary display, `**mapping` copies the mapping entries into the new dictionary.

prompts.label: READ OVERRIDE ORDER
prompts.placeholder: Click the later unpack. Later duplicate keys win.

annotations.title: Later mapping overrides earlier duplicates
annotations.explanation: timeout becomes 10 because environment appears after defaults.

annotations.title: Last duplicate wins
annotations.explanation: retries becomes 4 because override is last.

reveal.text: When a duplicate key appears in a dictionary display, the later value replaces the earlier value.

prompts.label: DO NOT CONFUSE CALL UNPACKING WITH DICT UNPACKING

glossary.definition: An object that associates keys with values. A dictionary is the most common mapping.
Curly-brace syntax such as `{key: value}` or `{**mapping}` that creates a new dictionary.
The same dictionary key appearing more than once while a dictionary is being built.

prompts.label: HOW DOES A TUPLE SORT KEY WORK?

reveal.text: A tuple key is compared lexicographically: Python compares fields from left to right until one differs.

reveal.code:
records = [
    {"team": "blue", "score": 8},
    {"team": "red", "score": 9},
    {"team": "blue", "score": 10},
]

ordered = sorted(
    records,
    key=lambda row: (row["team"], -row["score"]),
)

annotations.title: Key function
annotations.explanation: sorted compares the values returned by the key function.

annotations.title: Compound tuple key
annotations.explanation: Rows sort by team first, then by descending score within each team.

reveal.text: For numeric fields, negating one field reverses only that field inside an otherwise ascending tuple key.
Python sorting is stable, so multi-pass sorts can handle mixed directions without destroying earlier tie ordering.

glossary.definition: Compare items left to right and stop at the first position that differs.
A stable sort keeps the original relative order of items whose sort keys compare equal.
The function passed with `key=` that computes the value Python uses for sorting each item.
An ordered, immutable collection of values, usually written with commas.
